scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that too many options overwhelm while arguing too few can be just as harmful; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Standing before a huge menu, we sometimes wish there were only a few dishes to choose from.
One claim holds that it is better to have a limited number of options when deciding, on the reason that more options make a rational decision harder.
I agree that too many options can be overwhelming, but I do not believe fewer is always better.
First, there is real truth in the reason that too many options make deciding harder.
When choices pile up, people can feel confused, anxious, and unable to decide at all.
For example, a shopper faced with fifty brands may give up rather than compare them all.
This shows that too much choice can paralyse us rather than help us.
A smaller set of options lets us weigh each one carefully and choose with confidence.
Limiting choices can also save time and reduce needless stress.
To this extent, fewer options can genuinely help us decide.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why too few options harm

sentences.text: Second, however, having too few options can be just as harmful.
If choices are too narrow, we may be forced to accept something that suits us poorly.
Consider a patient given only one treatment when a better one exists but is not offered.
Such cases show that too little choice can deny us what we truly need.
A reasonable range of options also lets people match a decision to their own situation.
Freedom to choose among real alternatives is itself something people value deeply.
The best decisions, then, come from a sensible number of options, neither too many nor too few.
In conclusion, limiting options can help us avoid the confusion of too much choice.
But too few options can trap us with poor decisions and little freedom.
The wisest approach offers a reasonable range of choices, balanced between overload and too little freedom.
